snip.t: Persistence of an interatrial communication may be described as a patent foramen ovale; this is common in early life and is not equivalent to a haemodynamically significant congenital atrial septal defect.

snip.t: Ostium Primum Atrial Septal Defect (ASD): Occurs when the septum primum fails to fuse with the endocardial cushions (septum intermedium).
snip.s: Development of the Interatrial Septum — Study Notes

snip.t: Ostium Secundum Atrial Septal Defect (ASD): Caused by excessive apoptosis and resorption of the septum primum, or insufficient formation of the septum secundum.
snip.s: Development of the Interatrial Septum — Study Notes

snip.t: Ventricular septal defects (VSDs), Atrial septal defects (ASDs), Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): Abnormal blood flow can damage the endocardium.
Paradoxical embolism from deep venous thrombosis through an atrial septal defect
Congenital heart disease (about 20%), for example tetralogy of Fallot and atrial septal defect.
snip.s: Congenital Abdominal Wall Defects: Umbilical Hernia, Omphalocele and Gastroschis

snip.t: Conditions like atrial septal defect (ASD), myocardial infarction, and pericardial/myocardial diseases frequently precipitate atrial fibrillation.

qs.q: A researcher observes that the foramen ovale remains patent in a newborn despite normal postnatal pressure changes. Which structural characteristic distinguishes this condition from a true atrial septal defect?
o: It involves a hole in the septum primum rather than the secundum
It results from the failure of the ductus arteriosus to close properly
It is a flap-like opening where the septum primum acts as a valve
It is caused by excessive apoptosis of the endocardial cushion tissue
It involves a persistent connection between the sinus and atrium
qs.e: PFO is a functional closure failure of the flap valve, not a structural hole in the septum.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An infant is diagnosed with an isolated sinus venosus atrial septal defect. This specific lesion stems from an abnormality involving which embryonic venous structure integration?
o: Persistence of the umbilical vein connections
Abnormal regression of the left common cardinal
Excessive absorption of the vitelline channels
Stenosis of the anterior cardinal trunk lumen
Incomplete incorporation of the right horn
qs.e: The smooth part of the right atrium is formed by the incorporation of the right horn of the sinus venosus.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An infant is found to have a secundum atrial septal defect combined with abnormal drainage of the left superior vena cava. Which embryonic venous structure failed to regress normally?
o: Right anterior cardinal vein forming the jugular trunk
Left vitelline vein forming the portal sinus channel
Left common cardinal vein forming the oblique vein
Left umbilical vein forming the ligamentum teres
Right posterior cardinal vein forming the azygous root
qs.e: Persistence of the left common cardinal vein results in a persistent left superior vena cava draining into the coronary sinus.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which specific type of atrial septal defect is most frequently encountered in clinical practice?
o: Coronary sinus atrial septal defect
Ostium primum atrial septal defect
Sinus venosus atrial septal defect
Ostium secundum atrial septal defect
qs.e: Ostium secundum defects account for about 75% of all atrial septal defects and are the most common type. Sinus venosus and ostium primum types occur much less frequently.

qs.q: Which genetic syndrome is classically associated with an ostium primum atrial septal defect?
o: Associated with classic Marfan syndrome
Associated with classic Klinefelter syndrome
Associated with classic Turner syndrome
Associated with classic Down syndrome
qs.e: Ostium primum defects are closely associated with Down syndrome and atrioventricular valve clefts. Turner syndrome is instead commonly linked with coarctation of the aorta.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about atrial septal defects (ASD) is false?
o: Ostium secundum defects are the most common type
Ostium primum defects are located near the superior vena cava
ASDs can lead to paradoxical emboli and strokes
Most children with ASDs have normal growth and development
qs.e: Ostium primum defects are located near the atrioventricular valves, not the superior vena cava; ostium secundum defects are near the SVC. The other statements are true according to the note.

qs.q: Which physical examination finding is characteristic of an atrial septal defect (ASD)?
o: Continuous machinery murmur
Widened pulse pressure with low diastolic reading
Fixed widely split second heart sound
Pansystolic murmur at the apex
qs.e: An ASD causes a fixed widely split second heart sound because the right ventricle pumps more blood to the pulmonary artery, mimicking pulmonary valve stenosis. A continuous machinery murmur is specific to a PDA.

qs.q: A 4-year-old child is found to have an uncomplicated secundum atrial septal defect measuring 12 mm with right ventricular volume overload. What is the standard management approach for this finding?
o: Lifelong observation without any intervention
Emergency surgical closure in the neonatal period
Chronic medical therapy with digoxin and diuretics
Device closure via cardiac catheterization
qs.e: Most significant secundum atrial septal defects are closed by a device via cardiac catheterization around 3 to 6 years of age. Conversely, smaller defects may be observed, but significant volume overload requires intervention.

es.q: List and explain the two main types of atrial septal defects described in the notes.
es.m:
- **Key points:**
- Ostium primum ASD: failure of the septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions (septum intermedium).
- Ostium secundum ASD: excessive apoptosis/resorption of the septum primum or insufficient formation of the septum secundum.
- Both defects result in a permanent opening between the right and left atria.
- A patent foramen ovale (PFO) is a tunnel‑like passage, not a permanent opening.
- PFOs are often asymptomatic but may be associated with cryptogenic stroke.
es.s: Development of the Interatrial Septum: Essay questions

ai.title: Atrial Septal Defect
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A congenital hole between the atria that causes left‑to‑right shunt, leading to right‑heart overload. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and imaging; management ranges from monitoring to device or surgical closure.

sections.p: Atrial septal defect is a persistent opening in the interatrial septum allowing oxygen‑rich blood to flow from the left atrium to the right atrium.
b: Left‑to‑right shunt produces volume overload of the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation.
Most common type is ostium secundum; ostium primum is associated with atrioventricular canal defects.

t.b: Is there a fixed split S2? – A wide, fixed splitting of S2 suggests an ASD and indicates persistent left‑to‑right shunt.
What does the silhouette show? – Enlarged right heart border and increased pulmonary vascular markings support significant shunt.
Does the image confirm a defect and its size? – Direct visualization of the defect, direction of flow, and estimation of Qp:Qs ratio; Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5 : 1 indicates hemodynamically significant ASD.
What rhythm clues are present? – Right‑axis deviation and incomplete right bundle‑branch block are typical but not diagnostic.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the magnitude of the left‑to‑right shunt (Qp:Qs) and the impact on right‑heart size and function.
b: Mild: Qp:Qs < 1.5 : 1, normal RV size.
Moderate: Qp:Qs 1.5‑2 : 1, RV enlargement but preserved function.
Severe: Qp:Qs > 2 : 1, RV dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension.

sections.p: ASDs are primarily developmental, but in low‑resource settings consider associated conditions that may worsen presentation.
b: Ostium secundum defect – failure of septum primum resorption or septum secundum under‑development.
Ostium primum defect – incomplete fusion of endocardial cushions; often with AV valve cleft.
Associated congenital lesions – e.g., atrioventricular canal, tetralogy of Fallot.
Co‑existing infections – chronic malaria or HIV can increase pulmonary pressures, unmasking a previously silent ASD.

sections.p: Children may be asymptomatic early; later signs reflect right‑heart volume overload.
b: Exercise intolerance, easy fatigue.
Recurrent respiratory infections due to pulmonary congestion.
Growth failure if shunt is large.
Auscultation: wide, fixed split S2; systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there desaturation? – Normal saturation; desaturation suggests a right‑to‑left shunt or pulmonary hypertension.
Can the defect be visualized? – Confirms size, location, and shunt direction; essential before any closure decision.
What is the precise anatomy? – Useful when echo windows are poor; not required for routine care in low‑resource settings.
Are there co‑existing infections? – Anemia or malaria may worsen symptoms; treat before definitive cardiac intervention.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or intervention.
b: Pulmonary hypertension with right‑to‑left shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome).
Atrial arrhythmias (atrial flutter/fibrillation).
Heart failure signs: peripheral edema, hepatomegaly.
Paradoxical embolus causing stroke or systemic embolism.

sections.p: Treat associated conditions, monitor, and close the defect when indicated.
b: Medical: diuretics for symptomatic heart failure; anticoagulation only if atrial arrhythmia or paradoxical embolus.
Device closure: percutaneous occluder for secundum defects ≥ 5 mm with adequate rims; preferred in centers with catheter labs.
Surgical repair: required for large primum defects, inadequate rims, or when device closure is not feasible.
Avoid: routine long‑term anticoagulation in isolated ASD without arrhythmia due to bleeding risk.
Echocardiogram every 1‑2 years until closure; then at 5‑year intervals.
Monitor for pulmonary hypertension; treat early if pressures rise.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce respiratory infections.
Educate families about signs of arrhythmia or heart failure.
Patent ductus arteriosus – continuous murmur, left‑to‑right shunt at the ductus, not an atrial defect.
Ventricular septal defect – harsh holosystolic murmur, shunt at ventricular level.
Pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease – may also cause split S2 but lacks atrial shunt.
Normal chest X‑ray early in life may give false reassurance; defect can be silent until later.
ECG may be normal in small ASDs; do not rely on ECG alone to exclude disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden cyanosis or drop in oxygen saturation
Rapidly worsening dyspnea or chest pain

faq.q: Why is the split of S2 fixed in ASD?
faq.a: Because right‑ventricular systole is delayed by volume overload, keeping the pulmonic component consistently later regardless of breathing.

faq.q: When is device closure preferred over surgery?
faq.a: For secundum defects ≥5 mm with sufficient rim tissue and no associated cardiac anomalies, especially when catheter facilities exist.
Small secundum defects (<5 mm) may close in early childhood; larger defects rarely close without intervention.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect an ASD in a 6‑year‑old with recurrent cough? — Fixed split S2, systolic ejection murmur, and signs of right‑heart enlargement on exam.

How do you differentiate an ASD from a VSD using auscultation? — ASD gives a wide, fixed split S2 and a systolic ejection murmur; VSD produces a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
A child with known ASD develops cyanosis at rest. What is the most likely pathophysiology? — Development of Eisenmenger syndrome with reversal to right‑to‑left shunt.
When is closure of an ASD indicated in a resource‑limited setting? — When Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5 : 1, RV enlargement, symptoms, or pulmonary pressures are rising, and safe device or surgical options exist.
Why is routine anticoagulation not recommended for an isolated ASD? — The risk of bleeding outweighs the low baseline embolic risk without atrial arrhythmia.
What are the contraindications to percutaneous device closure? — Defect size >38 mm, inadequate rim tissue, associated primum defect, or pulmonary hypertension with reversed shunt.

How would you manage a patient with ASD and concurrent malaria infection awaiting closure? — Treat malaria promptly, monitor for anemia, and defer closure until infection resolves to reduce peri‑procedural risk.
What long‑term complication should you screen for after successful ASD closure? — Late arrhythmias, especially atrial flutter, and residual pulmonary hypertension.
